The Amazon milk frog Trachycephalus resinifictrix exhibits a life history shaped by its arboreal, phytotelm-breeding habits. Females deposit their clutches in water-filled tree cavities, where the aquatic larvae undergo development. At the time of hatching, neonates emerge after an incubation period of just 7 days [ab = 7 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. These newly hatched individuals are remarkably small, possessing a wet weight of only 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a mass that reflects the modest size of the yolk-laden egg from which they emerge. This rapid embryonic development, completing in roughly one week, is typical of many hylid frogs that exploit ephemeral arboreal water bodies where the window of opportunity for larval growth may be constrained. The tiny hatchlings must quickly transition to active feeding in their confined aquatic microhabitat, a selective pressure that likely drives the short incubation period observed in this species.

Following eclosion, the free-swimming tadpoles enter a period of rapid growth and morphological transformation. Under controlled laboratory conditions at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the time elapsed since birth at metamorphosis is approximately 56 days , a developmental duration that falls within the typical range of six to ten weeks reported for the species. By the culmination of this larval stage, the froglets have achieved a snout-vent length of 1.6 centimeters  and a corresponding wet weight of 0.393 grams . This complete body plan reorganisation involves the resorption of the tail, the development of functional limbs, and the transition from gill-based respiration to pulmonary gas exchange. The relatively brief larval period, coupled with the attainment of a modest body size at metamorphosis, is an adaptation to the temporary nature of their breeding sites, ensuring that young frogs emerge before the tree holes dry out.

After the terrestrial transition, the recently metamorphosed juveniles embark on a protracted period of somatic growth before reaching reproductive competence. This post-metamorphic developmental phase is notably lengthy for a frog of its size. In females, the time elapsed since metamorphosis at puberty is estimated at 547.5 days [tp = 547.5 days], or approximately one and a half years, under a thermal regime of 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. At the onset of sexual maturation, individuals of both sexes attain a snout-vent length of 5.25 centimeters [Lp = 5.25 centimeters], although it must be noted that this speculative value represents an approximation based on limited field data. This extended period of juvenile development allows the growing frog to accumulate sufficient body reserves and achieve the structural size necessary to support the energetic demands of future reproductive activity.

The Amazon milk frog displays considerable sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size, a common pattern among anurans where females are the larger sex. Adult females reach a maximum snout-vent length of 8.8 centimeters [Li = 8.8 centimeters], whereas males attain a smaller ultimate length of 7.7 centimeters [Li = 7.7 centimeters]. This disparity in length is mirrored by an even more pronounced divergence in body mass. The ultimate wet weight for females is 71 grams [Wwi = 71 grams], while males achieve a maximum adult body mass of 47.6 grams [Wwi = 47.6 grams]. The greater size of females is likely a consequence of fecundity selection, as a larger body cavity permits the production of a greater number of eggs per clutch. These asymptotic values represent the maximum sizes recorded from long-term field studies and captive colonies, and they provide a benchmark for assessing individual growth trajectories.

Reproductive output in Trachycephalus resinifictrix is characterised by a single, large annual clutch. Females lay approximately 2,500 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 2,500 eggs per clutch], and they typically produce just a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] when maintained under stable thermal conditions at 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This reproductive strategy, featuring high fecundity concentrated in one annual event, is consistent with an explosive breeding pattern typical of many Neotropical hylids. Finally, the species exhibits a maximum lifespan of 8,030 days [am = 8,030 days], equivalent to approximately 22 years, under captive conditions at 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This remarkable longevity is exceptional among anurans and likely reflects the low extrinsic mortality rates associated with their arboreal, chemically defended lifestyle in a relatively predator-reduced canopy environment.
